summary: Specifies the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol, based on the One-way Active Measurement Protocol, for measuring round-trip or two-way network metrics between two devices. OWAMP could be used both ways for one-way metrics but could not handle round trips. TWAMP is standards-track and has been extended later.

plainLanguage.summary: TWAMP lets two devices measure how long a message takes to go back and forth across a network. One device sends a packet, the other stamps it and sends it back immediately, so travel time can be calculated accurately.

questions: how to measure round trip delay between network devices
subtitle: A two-way active measurement protocol to measure round-trip delay and related metrics between two devices.

tldr.problem: OWAMP provides one-way measurements but does not support round-trip or two-way measurements directly.
tldr.mechanism: TWAMP uses a Control protocol to set up sessions and a Test protocol where a Session-Reflector returns received packets with timestamps so both directions can be measured.
tldr.outcome: TWAMP enables two-way active measurement of delay and related metrics without requiring synchronized clocks at both ends. It is a Proposed Standard updated by later RFCs.

today: RFC 5357 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 5618, RFC 5938, RFC 6038, RFC 7717, RFC 7750 and RFC 8545.

sections.title: Why a Two-Way Protocol
sections.content:
The One-way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP, RFC 4656) provides one-way measurements. While OWAMP can be run in both directions, it does not directly provide round-trip or two-way measurements. RFC 5357 defines the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP) to add that capability.

Two-way measurements are common in IP networks. For round-trip delay, the clocks at the two ends do not need to be synchronized. TWAMP builds on OWAMP's architecture and design, adding timestamps applied at the reflector so processing delays can be accounted for.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring a round trip is useful because you do not need both clocks to agree. TWAMP sends a message, has the other end mark when it arrived and send it right back, so you can tell how long the round trip took.

sections.title: Roles and Protocols
sections.content:
TWAMP has two interrelated protocols: TWAMP-Control initiates, starts, and stops test sessions, and TWAMP-Test exchanges test packets between two TWAMP entities.

The roles follow OWAMP with changes: the Session-Receiver becomes the Session-Reflector, which creates and sends a measurement packet when it receives one but does not collect results. There is no Fetch-Client. A typical two-host setup puts the Control-Client and Session-Sender on one host and the Server and Session-Reflector on the other.
sections.plainLanguage: One device runs the control side and sends test packets. The other device reflects packets back immediately while recording when they arrived. This lets round-trip times be measured cleanly.

sections.title: Control Connection
sections.content:
The Control-Client opens a TCP connection to the Server on well-known port 862. The Server sends a Greeting listing supported security modes. The client chooses a mode; the Server accepts and returns its start time. The client may request test sessions, send Start-Sessions to begin them, and later Stop-Sessions to end them.

The Control-Client MAY set a Diffserv Code Point (DSCP) on control packets; the Server SHOULD reuse the DSCP from the client's TCP SYN. To free resources on failure, the Server MAY drop a control connection silent for SERVWAIT seconds (default 900), and the Session-Reflector MAY drop a session silent for REFWAIT seconds (default 900).
sections.plainLanguage: The two devices first talk over a control connection to agree on how testing will work. If either side stops responding, they time out after a while to free up resources.

sections.title: Requesting and Stopping Sessions
sections.content:
TWAMP defines Request-TW-Session (Command Number 5) instead of OWAMP's Request-Session. The Fetch-Session command is not used. For Request-TW-Session, Conf-Sender and Conf-Receiver MUST both be 0; Number of Scheduled Slots and Number of Packets MUST be 0; and the SID MUST be 0 (the Server assigns it). The sender and reflector each use their own UDP port for test packets. The Timeout field tells the reflector how long to keep reflecting packets in transit after Stop-Sessions.

The sender chooses its own send schedule. The reflector SHOULD return each packet as quickly as possible. Stop-Sessions (Command Number 3) comes only from the Control-Client and applies to all sessions started.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender tells the reflector what ports to use for the test. The reflector just sends every received test packet back right away, following simple rules.

sections.title: Test Packets and Reflector Behavior
sections.content:
TWAMP-Test has two packet formats (sender and reflector). For each received test packet, the reflector MUST record the arrival time (Receive Timestamp), copy the sender's sequence number and timestamp/error estimate, set Sender TTL from the received packet's TTL or Hop Limit (or 255 if unavailable), and transmit the reflected packet as immediately as possible with its own Timestamp.

The reflector gives each reflected packet its own independent sequence number starting at zero. To make packet sizes equal in both directions, the sender may append padding (at least 27 octets in unauthenticated mode, at least 56 in authenticated/encrypted modes). Padding is not covered by HMAC or encryption. Authenticated and encrypted modes use AES-based protection as specified in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: When the reflector gets a test packet, it writes down when it arrived, copies the sender's notes, adds its own send time, and throws it back right away. This lets the sender figure out the round-trip time and how long the reflector took.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TWAMP inherits OWAMP's security considerations; the change from receiver to reflector does not introduce new known vulnerabilities. The Server-Greeting includes a 32-bit PKCS #5 iteration counter (Count) used to derive keys. An attacker could set a very large value and cause the receiver to spend significant time generating keys.

To mitigate this, TWAMP systems SHOULD have a configuration control limiting the maximum Count value, with a default maximum of 32768. If a Control-Client receives a Count greater than its configured maximum, it SHOULD close the control connection.
sections.plainLanguage: To avoid wasting time on a very long computation, systems set a reasonable upper limit on how much work they will do to generate keys. If asked to do too much, they stop.
